c.tagline: Europe's oldest city, wrapped by Atlantic beaches and Carnival spirit.

taxi.fareNote: Official white taxis with a red stripe; fares are metered with surcharges for night, weekends, luggage, and airport/station pickups.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU emergency number covering police, fire, and ambulance.

avoid.reason: Pickpockets work the packed Carnival crowds and summer beach promenades; watch belongings at La Caleta.

hood_desc: Cadiz's oldest quarter, wedged inside three medieval Roman-era gates, with narrow lanes leading to the excavated Teatro Romano. It feels like a living archaeological site, with faded facades and quiet, atmospheric plazas.

The fiercely traditional fishing barrio that is the beating heart of Cadiz's famous Carnival, packed with tiny tapas bars and freidurias serving fried fish straight from the bay. It backs onto Playa de la Caleta, the city's most photogenic beach.

A working-class neighborhood long associated with flamenco, home to intimate peñas (flamenco clubs) where you can hear authentic cante flamenco. It's grittier and less touristy than the surrounding old town.

A lively, central district built around the Gran Teatro Falla and bustling squares like Plaza de la Merced, mixing everyday local life with theatre-going crowds. Its markets and shops make it a good base for exploring on foot.
The postcard beach neighborhood between two 16th-century castles, Santa Catalina and San Sebastian, where locals swim, stroll the seafront promenade, and watch the Atlantic sunset.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink, though some prefer bottled for taste.

transit.pay: Cash or contactless on TUC city buses; ferry tickets bought at the dock
transit.note: The old town is compact and best explored on foot; a small passenger ferry (El Vapor) crosses the bay to El Puerto de Santa Maria.

train: High-speed AVE/Avant and regional trains to Seville and Madrid from Cadiz station
bus: ALSA intercity coaches to Seville, Malaga, and beyond
ferry: Local passenger ferry (El Vapor) to El Puerto de Santa Maria

tip.r: Rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service is appreciated but not expected; service charge is included in prices.

landmarks: Catedral de Cádiz (Cadiz Cathedral)
Its gleaming golden dome dominates the skyline of Europe's oldest city, a baroque-neoclassical colossus whose Levante tower rewards climbers with sweeping Atlantic panoramas.
Torre Tavira
The tallest of Cádiz's 18th-century merchant watchtowers hides a magical camera obscura that projects live, moving images of the white city onto a concave screen.
Playa de la Caleta
Cradled between two castles where fishing boats bob at anchor, this golden cove starred as Havana in a Bond film and delivers legendary sunsets.
Castillo de San Sebastián
Reached by a romantic stone causeway jutting into the Atlantic, this island fortress marks the mythical site of a temple to the Phoenician god Melqart.
Castillo de Santa Catalina
A star-shaped 1598 fortress guarding La Caleta's northern flank, its ramparts, chapel, and art exhibitions offer free entry and crashing-wave views.
Teatro Romano (Roman Theatre)
Discovered by accident in 1980 beneath the Pópulo quarter, this 1st-century BC theatre was among the Roman world's largest, seating some 20,000 spectators.
Plaza de España and the 1812 Constitution Monument
A soaring marble-and-bronze monument celebrates the liberal constitution Cádiz gave Spain in 1812, presiding over an elegant palm-fringed square near the port.
Mercado Central de Abastos
Spain's oldest covered market buzzes inside a neoclassical colonnade, where stalls piled with tuna and shrimp fritters feed the city's irresistible tapas culture.
Parque Genovés
A whimsical 19th-century garden of sculpted cypresses, dragon trees, and a waterfall grotto, spread along the seafront ramparts on the old town's edge.
Barrio del Pópulo
Cádiz's oldest quarter squeezes medieval arches, the Roman theatre, and flower-hung lanes into a few atmospheric blocks between cathedral and sea.

train.note: No international trains. Cádiz sits at the end of the line on its narrow spit, with Alvia long-distance services to Madrid in about 4 hours and frequent Cercanías C-1 trains up the bay to Jerez, El Puerto de Santa María and San Fernando. The station is beside the port at the edge of the old town. Booking opens around 60 days ahead.

bus.note: No international coaches leave Cádiz directly - Morocco services run from Algeciras or Tarifa, about 90 minutes south. Comes and ALSA (https://www.alsa.com/en) run from the bus station next to the railway terminus to Seville (about 1h45), Tarifa, Algeciras and the Costa de la Luz beaches.

intl.to: Canary Islands - Tenerife, Las Palmas & La Palma (Spain) - ~40 hr weekly sailing
El Puerto de Santa María & Rota (Spain) - across the bay
intl.op: Catamarán de la Bahía (Consorcio de Transportes)

ferry.note: Cádiz is the mainland's main link to the Canary Islands, with a weekly Trasmediterránea sailing that takes the best part of two days and carries cars - it is slower than flying but the only way to bring a vehicle. The little catamaran across the bay to El Puerto de Santa María is a 30-minute commuter run on an ordinary transit fare and a lovely way to reach the sherry towns.

half.name: Jerez de la Frontera
half.blurb: Sherry-producing city famous for its bodegas, flamenco heritage and the Royal Andalusian School of Equestrian Art.

half.name: Seville
half.blurb: Andalusian capital with the Gothic cathedral, Alcázar palace and Plaza de España, under two hours by train.

half.name: Tarifa
half.blurb: Windsurfing hub at Europe's southernmost tip, where the Atlantic meets the Mediterranean within sight of Morocco.

half.name: Vejer de la Frontera
half.blurb: Whitewashed hill town of narrow lanes above the Costa de la Luz, one of Andalusia's classic pueblos blancos.
